sections.body:
A vegetable is the part of a plant that we eat, but we do not eat the seeds. Vegetables grow in the ground, on a stalk or on a bush. A carrot grows under the soil. A cabbage grows in the soil. Tomatoes and eggplants grow on a plant above the ground.

Vegetables come in many colours. Some are green, like morning glory and broccoli. Some are red, like a tomato. Some are orange, like a carrot or a pumpkin. Some are white, like a turnip or a mushroom.

Every vegetable has a part that we call the **root**, the **leaf** or the **stalk**. A carrot is a root. Morning glory and cabbage are leaves. Bok choy and broccoli grow on a stalk.

Vegetables are good for your body. They fill your tummy without making you heavy. They have **vitamins**, which are tiny helpers that keep you well. They also have fibre, which helps your tummy work.

Vegetables taste best when they are cooked just a little. Too much cooking takes away the vitamins. So many families stir-fry vegetables for only a few minutes.

And vegetables belong to every meal. They sit next to the rice on the plate. They make the meal colourful and they make it complete.
examples: This is a carrot. It is a root.
Broccoli is green, and carrots are orange.
I eat vegetables with rice at lunch.
sections.heading: What is a vegetable?

sections.body:
Green vegetables are the ones people buy most. Morning glory, broccoli, spinach, green beans and Chinese cabbage are all green. Green vegetables help your eyes stay strong.

Red vegetables give your body warmth. A tomato is red. A red chilli is small but strong. Beetroot is deep red inside.

Orange and **yellow** vegetables keep your skin and your teeth bright. A carrot, a pumpkin and sweet corn are orange or yellow. Carrots are famous for helping your eyes.

White and **brown** vegetables are gentle and filling. A turnip is white. A potato is brown outside and white inside. A mushroom is white and brown too.

Purple vegetables are a fun surprise. Eggplant is purple. Purple onion is purple. They are very good for you.

Here is a small idea to try. At one meal, pick one vegetable of each colour. You can put green morning glory, red tomato and orange carrot in one bowl. It looks like a rainbow, and it tastes good too.
examples: A pumpkin is orange, and a tomato is red.
I made a rainbow bowl with three colours.
sections.heading: Vegetables come in many colours

sections.body:
Vegetables come from the ground and from the market. They carry dust, so you always wash them well.

First, wash your hands with soap. Then rinse the vegetables under running water. Leafy greens need a little more care, because dirt hides in the folds.

Next, put them on a clean board. Use a clean knife. Cut away any part that is brown or dry.

Then cut them the way you want. Cut leaves into strips. Cut a carrot into thin rounds. Cut cabbage into small pieces. Cut a pumpkin into small cubes, and ask an adult to help.

After that, cook them fast. Put a little oil in the pan. Cook the vegetables for only three or four minutes, and keep the lid on. They stay bright, crunchy and full of vitamins.

Last, taste one before you serve it. If it is still hard, cook it a little longer. Then bring it to the table.
examples: I wash the vegetables before Dad cooks them.
I cut the carrot into thin rounds.
We stir-fry the greens for three minutes.
sections.heading: How to help prepare vegetables
steps: Rinse the vegetables under running water.
Cut them on a clean board with a clean knife.
Stir-fry for only three or four minutes.
Taste one piece before you serve it.

sections.body:
Grown-ups use special words for vegetables. Here are the ones you will hear most.

A **vegetable** is a plant we eat for the part that is not the seed. Carrot, cabbage and tomato are all vegetables.

A **root** is the part of a vegetable that grows under the soil. Carrot, radish, turnip and potato are roots. Roots are strong and they hold a lot of goodness.

A **leaf** is the flat green part of a vegetable. Cabbage, spinach and morning glory are leaves. Leaves are light and full of vitamins.

A **stalk** is the firm stem that holds leaves up. Broccoli and bok choy grow on a stalk. It is the part you eat with the leaves.

Stir-fry means to cook small pieces of food quickly in a little oil over a hot fire. Vegetables stay crunchy and colourful this way. It is the most common way to cook vegetables in Vietnam, and it takes about five minutes.
examples: A carrot is a root vegetable.
The leaves are very fresh today.
sections.heading: The words we use for vegetables

terms.example: Broccoli and carrot are both vegetables.

sections.body:
Vegetables are good for you, but a few things need care.

Vegetables grow in the soil, so they can carry **germs**. Wash them well every time, even the ones you peel. Wash them under running water, not in a bowl of still water.

Some vegetables are **raw** only in small amounts. A green sprouting shoot is not the same as a bean sprout, and it can make your tummy hurt. If you are not sure, ask an adult.

Be careful with the knife. Cut on a flat board, keep your fingers back, and let an adult help with hard vegetables like pumpkin and coconut.

And watch out for **peanuts and shellfish**. Some sauces and stock cubes have peanuts or shrimp in them. A person with an allergy can become very ill from a tiny amount.

If a vegetable smells strange, feels slimy, or has gone dark and soft, throw it away. Good food is worth waiting for.
examples: I wash the vegetables under the tap.
Mom helps me cut the pumpkin.
This sauce has peanuts in it, so I cannot eat it.
sections.heading: Some vegetables need care

sections.body:
In Vietnam, vegetables are always at the table. A family meal usually has rice, a dish of protein, and a plate or bowl of vegetables.

Rau muống is the most loved green. It grows fast in the wet season. People stir-fry it with garlic, or boil it and pour fish sauce on top.

Cà chua is eaten in many ways. It is a tomato, and it goes into soup, into a stir-fry, and straight onto a plate of noodles.

Cà rốt is a root. It is often shredded into salad, or cooked with a little sugar in a soup for children.

Bắp cải is a cabbage. It is boiled and eaten with a dipping sauce, or cooked slowly with meat.

Cà chua xanh and **đậu bắp** are common at a small market. A green tomato is used in a sour soup, and baby corn is cooked whole.

Vegetables are not only for dinner. Many families eat a bowl of clear soup with vegetables in the middle of the day. Some children eat a piece of cucumber or a tomato as a snack.

Try this at home. Count the vegetables on the dinner table today. Then ask which colour each one is. You will be surprised how many colours there are.
examples: We eat rau muống with garlic.
Cà chua goes into the soup.
I ate a piece of cucumber as a snack.
sections.heading: Vegetables in a Vietnamese meal

item.summary: Vegetables are the colourful parts of plants that we eat. After reading this you can name vegetables by their colours, say where they grow, and help prepare a simple dish at home.
item.title: Vegetables and Their Colors
